  %\VignetteIndexEntry{Effort: how hard the model reasons}

```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

A reasoning model works through a request in text you never see before it
writes the reply. The provider bills that text as output and counts it inside
the reply's output cap. The reasoning effort tells the model how much of it to
do: `"low"` for a quick answer, `"high"` for a request that needs more
thought.

harnessr sends no effort unless you ask for one, and each request then goes
out at the provider's default. This guide covers how to ask:

- which models take an effort, and what happens with one that does not;
- one effort for every call, or one per stage of your code;
- what effort does to the cost, the response cache and the trace;
- effort that starts low and rises for the next stage only when something
  went wrong, with `hr_effort_escalate()`, `hr_effort_event()` and
  `hr_effort_log()`;
- measuring whether that saves money without losing answers, with
  `hr_effort_check()`.

Every example runs offline with no API key. The calls that would reach a real
provider are shown but not run.

## Setting up

```{r message = FALSE}
library(harnessr)
old <- hr_options(verbose = FALSE)
```

`hr_options()` returns the values it replaced, and the last chunk of this guide
puts them back with `hr_options(old)`.

The examples use a stand-in reasoning model. Its prices are illustrative and
appear so that the costs below are not `NA`; use your provider's current
prices for a real model:

```{r}
# Illustrative figures, in USD per million tokens.
hr_register_model("reasoner", context_window = 32000, max_output = 8000,
                  input_usd = 1, output_usd = 4, reasoning = TRUE)
```

## Which models take an effort

harnessr sends an effort only to a model whose registry entry says it reasons.
`hr_models()` has a `reasoning` column, and `hr_model_info()` gives one
model's flag:

```{r}
m <- hr_models()
m$id[m$reasoning %in% TRUE]
hr_model_info("gpt-5.6-luna")$reasoning
hr_model_info("gpt-4o")$reasoning
```

A model you register is a reasoning model when you say so with
`reasoning = TRUE`, as `"reasoner"` above. `vignette("models")` covers
registering a model.

A stand-in client shows what each call was sent. `hr_mock_client()` hands its
function the effort in `params$effort`:

```{r}
effort_seen <- hr_mock_client(function(messages, params) {
  paste("effort:", if (is.null(params$effort)) "none" else params$effort)
})
hr_call(effort_seen, "What was revenue in 2024?", model = "reasoner", effort = "low")$text
hr_call(effort_seen, "What was revenue in 2024?", model = "gpt-4o", effort = "low")$text
```

gpt-4o does not reason, so harnessr left the effort out of its request, with
no warning. A provider refuses an effort sent to such a model, and leaving it
out lets one setting cover a run that sends some requests to a cheap model
that does not reason and others to one that does. The trace records the effort
each request carried (see [Effort in the trace](#trace)).

A model the registry does not list is guessed. An id that matches a family
pattern takes the family's flag, so a new `gpt-5` model counts as reasoning,
and any other id gets the default entry, with `reasoning = FALSE`, and is sent
no effort until you register it:

```{r}
suppressWarnings(c(new_gpt5 = hr_model_info("gpt-5.9-preview")$reasoning,
                   unknown = hr_model_info("house-model")$reasoning))
```

### The levels

harnessr knows six levels: `"none"`, `"minimal"`, `"low"`, `"medium"`,
`"high"` and `"xhigh"`. Which of them a model accepts is the provider's rule.
`"none"` is a level the request carries, asking for no reasoning; leaving
`effort` unset sends no level at all.

A level harnessr does not know is sent as given, since providers add levels,
with a warning of class `gr_effort_unknown`. When the level is close to a known
one, the warning names it, because the provider would refuse every request a
typo goes out with:

```{r}
res <- withCallingHandlers(
  hr_call(effort_seen, "What was revenue in 2024?", model = "reasoner", effort = "hihg"),
  gr_effort_unknown = function(w) {
    message(conditionMessage(w))
    invokeRestart("muffleWarning")
  })
res$text
```

A setting of the wrong shape stops before anything is sent, with an error of
class `gr_bad_setting`: a value that is not text, a blank or missing value,
two values for the calls no name covers, or a name given twice.

```{r}
tryCatch(hr_call(effort_seen, "hi", model = "reasoner", effort = c("low", "high")),
         gr_bad_setting = function(e) "refused: two values with no names")
```

`effort` follows `...` in `hr_call()`, so name it in full.

## Where the effort goes in a request

An `hr_client()` puts the effort in the field its API reads:
`reasoning = list(effort = ...)` on the Responses API, and `reasoning_effort`
on Chat Completions. A mock or backend handler finds it in `params$effort`, as
above.

A client can carry a default effort of its own in `extra_body`, which goes on
every request it sends. The `effort` of a call is more specific, so it wins
for that call, and the rest of the client's `reasoning` object is kept:

```{r eval = FALSE}
cl <- hr_client(api = "responses",
                extra_body = list(reasoning = list(effort = "low", summary = "auto")))
# Sent with reasoning = {effort: "low", summary: "auto"}.
hr_call(cl, "Summarise the notes.", model = "gpt-5.6-luna")
# Sent with reasoning = {effort: "high", summary: "auto"}.
hr_call(cl, "Check the summary against the notes.", model = "gpt-5.6-luna",
        effort = "high")
```

The trace's `effort` column and the escalation policy below read the call's
`effort`, so they do not see an `extra_body` effort; only the step's
`params_sent`, the request as it went out, shows it. It is part of the client,
so it does change the response cache key. Prefer the call's `effort` when you
want the record to show it.

An `hr_ellmer_client()` cannot take an effort per call, because ellmer sets
it on the chat object. The first call through the client that asks for one
warns with class `gr_effort_unsupported`, and every call goes out at the
chat's own setting. Build the chat with the effort you want:

```{r eval = FALSE}
chat <- ellmer::chat_openai(model = "gpt-5.6-luna")
el <- hr_ellmer_client(chat)
hr_call(el, "Summarise the notes.", model = "gpt-5.6-luna", effort = "low")
#> Warning: Reasoning effort is set on the ellmer chat object, not per call, ...
```

The trace step of such a call keeps the effort it asked for as
`params$unsent_effort`, not `params$effort`, so the trace does not claim an
effort the request never carried.

## One effort for every call, or one per stage

Give `effort` one level and every call it is passed to goes out at that level.
harnessr has no session-wide effort option in `hr_options()`: the effort is a
setting of each call. To keep one effort across your code, hold it in one
place and pass it to each call, for example as an arm's setting that each call
reads (see [Does more effort pay?](#check)), or as a client's `extra_body`.

Calls in a run differ. A run that reads forty chunks and then writes one
answer makes forty small requests and one that judges. Name each call with
`label`, and give `effort` a character vector named by label:

```{r}
by_stage <- c(extract = "low", synthesise = "medium", "synthesise.section" = "high")
labels <- c("extract.chunk", "synthesise.merge.level2", "synthesise.section",
            "outline", "extractor")
vapply(labels, function(l) {
  hr_call(effort_seen, "hi", model = "reasoner", label = l, effort = by_stage)$text
}, character(1))
```

The rules the output follows:

- A name covers a label equal to it, or one that starts with it and a dot.
  `extract` covers `extract.chunk` but not `extractor`.
- When several names cover a label, the longest wins:
  `synthesise.section` goes out at `"high"` and the merge under `synthesise`
  at `"medium"`.
- An unnamed value, or one named `"default"`, covers every label no name
  covers. With none, as here, such a call is sent no effort: `outline` and
  `extractor` went out at the provider's default.

```{r}
hr_call(effort_seen, "hi", model = "reasoner", label = "outline",
        effort = c(extract = "low", default = "medium"))$text
```

`hr_call()` does not check the names against your labels. A misspelt name
covers no call, and those calls go out at the provider's default with nothing
said:

```{r}
hr_call(effort_seen, "hi", model = "reasoner", label = "extract.chunk",
        effort = c(extrac = "low"))$text
```

Check the trace's `effort` column after a first run. The document layer checks
its own maps against the labels its readers declare (see
[Where the document layer builds on this](#document-layer)).

## What effort costs

Reasoning is output. The provider counts the reasoning tokens inside the
reply's `output` tokens and bills them at the output price, so a higher effort
costs more on every request it reaches. A provider that reports them puts the
reasoning count in `usage$reasoning`, as part of `output`.

Here a backend stands in for a provider that reasons more at a higher effort
and reports what it spent:

```{r}
thinking <- c(low = 200L, medium = 800L, high = 3000L)
thinks <- hr_backend_client(function(messages, params) {
  r <- if (is.null(params$effort)) 1500L else thinking[[params$effort]]
  structure(list(ok = TRUE, text = "Revenue was 45.2 million dollars.",
                 usage = list(input = 120L, output = r + 9L, reasoning = r,
                              provenance = "reported")),
            class = "gr_result")
})
tr <- hr_trace()
for (e in c("low", "medium", "high")) {
  hr_call(thinks, "What was revenue in 2024?", model = "reasoner", effort = e,
          trace = tr, label = paste0("ask.", e))
}
invisible(hr_call(thinks, "What was revenue in 2024?", model = "reasoner",
                  trace = tr, label = "ask.unset"))
as.data.frame(tr)[, c("stage", "effort", "tokens_out", "tokens_reasoning", "usd")]
```

The reply is nine tokens each time, and the cost follows the reasoning. Unset,
the request went out at the provider's default, which this stand-in puts
between medium and high. A real provider's default is its own, so measure it
rather than assume it is cheap. The figures in `tokens_reasoning` and `usd`
come from what the provider reports; `hr_estimate_cost()` prices any count you
give it, reasoning included in `output_tokens`:

```{r}
hr_estimate_cost("reasoner", input_tokens = 120, output_tokens = 3009)
```

### Reasoning and the output cap

The output cap bounds the reasoning and the reply together. A request at
`"high"` with a small cap can spend the whole cap reasoning and come back cut
off, with `finish_reason` `"length"` and little or no text. A cut-off reply is
not cached, so a second run asks again.

harnessr guards against this for short requests. An HTTP request to a
reasoning model is sent with a cap of at least `hr_options("reasoning_floor")`
tokens, 2,048 by default, where the model's limit and the context window leave
room. The cache key, the trace's `params$max_output` and a mock or backend
handler see the cap you asked for; the trace's `params_sent` records the cap
the HTTP request carried, and the spending limits check the request at that
cap. [The output cap floor](#set-reasoning-floor) below covers the setting.

## Effort and the response cache

The effort a request carries is part of the response cache key, as the
temperature is, so replies at two efforts are never traded:

```{r}
n <- 0
counting <- hr_mock_client(function(messages, params) {
  n <<- n + 1
  "Revenue was 45.2 million dollars."
})
cache <- hr_cache(file.path(tempdir(), "effort-guide-cache"))
cached <- hr_cache_client(counting, cache)
c(low       = hr_call(cached, "What was revenue?", model = "reasoner", effort = "low")$cached,
  low_again = hr_call(cached, "What was revenue?", model = "reasoner", effort = "low")$cached,
  high      = hr_call(cached, "What was revenue?", model = "reasoner", effort = "high")$cached,
  unset     = hr_call(cached, "What was revenue?", model = "reasoner")$cached)
n
```

Three requests reached the model: the repeat at `"low"` came from the cache,
and `"high"` and the unset call each missed. The key holds the effort the
request carried, not the one the call asked for, so a model that does not
reason shares one entry whatever effort you pass:

```{r}
c(gpt4o_high  = hr_call(cached, "What was revenue?", model = "gpt-4o", effort = "high")$cached,
  gpt4o_unset = hr_call(cached, "What was revenue?", model = "gpt-4o")$cached)
```

With no effort set, the key has no effort part, so a cache written before you
used effort still answers calls that use none. A replay matches each call on
its effort too, and a call at an effort the recording does not hold stops with
an error of class `gr_replay_miss` that names the efforts it does hold:

```{r}
f <- tempfile(fileext = ".json")
hr_trace_save(tr, f)
rp <- hr_replay_client(f)
hr_call(rp, "What was revenue in 2024?", model = "reasoner", effort = "low",
        label = "ask.low")$text
tryCatch(hr_call(rp, "What was revenue in 2024?", model = "reasoner", effort = "xhigh"),
         gr_replay_miss = function(e) conditionMessage(e))
```

## Effort in the trace {#trace}

Each request's trace step keeps the effort it carried in `params$effort`, and
leaves the field out when it carried none:

```{r}
str(tr$steps[[1]]$params)
str(tr$steps[[4]]$params)
```

`as.data.frame()` of a trace has an `effort` column only when some request
carried an effort, so a trace without effort reads as it did before effort
existed. `NA` in the column marks a request sent no effort, such as the unset
call above or a request to a model that does not reason. A run that raises its
effort adds `"effort.escalate"` and `"effort.resolve"` steps, and
`hr_effort_event()` adds `"effort.event"` steps; both are covered next.

## Effort that rises only when needed

A fixed `"high"` pays for reasoning on every request, including the many that
a low effort answers as well. A fixed `"low"` saves that, and loses the
requests that needed more. `hr_effort_escalate()` builds a policy in between:
every stage starts at a base effort, and when something went wrong in one
stage, the next stage is sent at a raised effort.

```{r}
pol <- hr_effort_escalate(base = "low", to = "high",
                          replies = c(not_in_document = "NOT FOUND"))
pol
```

Pass the policy as a call's `effort`, with the same trace on every call of the
run. The policy keeps its state on the trace: which stage the run is in,
whether it was raised and how many raises are left. A call with no trace is
sent at the base effort.

Its arguments:

- `base`: the starting effort, one level or a map named by label, resolved as
  a fixed effort is.
- `to`: the raised effort, one level.
- `on`: the triggers that raise the next stage, all seven by default.
- `max_escalations`: the most raises in one run (one trace), 1 by default.
- `replies`: reply texts that count as triggers, named by trigger.

### Stages

A stage is a call label up to its second dot, with a merge level
(`.level2`), a summary level (`.L2`) or a judge's order (`.o2`) at the end
left off. `map.answer` and `reduce` are stages, and `reduce.level1` belongs to
`reduce`. The effort changes only when a call starts a new stage, never part
way through one, so the requests of one stage share an effort and a
provider's prompt cache.

`hr_call()` labels a call `"call"` unless you give a `label`, so a run of
unlabelled calls is one stage and is never raised. Label each stage.

### Triggers

The core sees three triggers for itself:

- `"truncated"`: a `"truncate"` step on the trace, which `hr_truncate()` and
  `hr_context_fit()` write when given the trace (see `vignette("context")`),
  or a reply cut off at its output cap.
- `"parse_failure"`: a reply to one of harnessr's own structured requests
  that is not JSON. These are `ctx$call_json()` in a benchmark arm, a judge
  and the document readers.
- `"schema_failure"`: such a reply that does not fit its schema.

`hr_call(schema = )` does not parse its reply, so a reply to it never fires
either trigger by itself. Check the reply in your code and report it with
`hr_effort_event()`, as [Reporting a trigger](#report-trigger) shows.

`replies` turns a reply into a trigger. With
`c(not_in_document = "NOT FOUND")`, the trigger fires when every request
of a stage replied with text that starts with `NOT FOUND`. The other
default triggers, `"verify_failed"`, `"unclear"` and `"disagreement"`, and any
name of your own, fire when your code reports them with `hr_effort_event()`.

### A raise, step by step

The stand-in below finds nothing at low effort when asked to find something,
and answers at any other effort:

```{r}
finder <- hr_mock_client(function(messages, params) {
  if (startsWith(messages[[1]]$content, "Find") && identical(params$effort, "low")) {
    return("NOT FOUND")
  }
  paste("answered at", params$effort)
})
tr <- hr_trace()
step <- function(prompt, label) {
  hr_call(finder, prompt, model = "reasoner", trace = tr, label = label, effort = pol)$text
}
step("Find the revenue figure in part 1.", "find.part1")
step("Find the revenue figure in part 2.", "find.part2")
step("Check the figure.", "check")
step("Write the answer.", "answer")
as.data.frame(tr)[, c("step", "stage", "effort", "reply")]
```

Stage `find.part1` went out low, and its only request replied
`NOT FOUND`. When `find.part2` started, the policy saw the trigger and
sent that stage high, where it found the figure. With one raise allowed and
used, `check` and `answer` went back to low. The step numbers skip 2 and 4:
those are the policy's own steps.

### The log: `hr_effort_log()`

`hr_effort_log()` returns one row per raise:

```{r}
hr_effort_log(tr)
```

`after` is the stage the triggers fired in, `stage` the stage sent raised,
`calls` the requests the raised stage sent and `resolved` whether the raised
stage fired none of the same triggers. `TRUE` here: at high effort the search
found what low effort missed. A raise whose stage is the last of the run is
settled from the trace as it is when you ask.

The trace holds the same facts as an `"effort.escalate"` step at the raise and
an `"effort.resolve"` step when the raised stage ends:

```{r}
local_steps <- Filter(function(s) identical(s$kind, "local"), tr$steps)
for (s in local_steps) {
  cat(s$label, ": ", paste(names(s$detail), unlist(s$detail), sep = " = ", collapse = "; "),
      "\n", sep = "")
}
```

### Reporting a trigger: `hr_effort_event()` {#report-trigger}

Some trouble only your code can see: two reviewers that disagree, a quotation
that failed a check. `hr_effort_event()` records it as an `"effort.event"`
step, and the policy reads it at the next stage boundary. This policy allows
two raises, starts the `draft` stage at low and every other stage at medium:

```{r}
pol2 <- hr_effort_escalate(base = c(draft = "low", default = "medium"), to = "xhigh",
                           max_escalations = 2)
cut_off <- hr_backend_client(function(messages, params) {
  long <- grepl("long", messages[[1]]$content) && !identical(params$effort, "xhigh")
  structure(list(ok = TRUE, text = paste("at", params$effort),
                 finish_reason = if (long) "length" else "stop",
                 usage = list(input = 10L, output = 5L)),
            class = "gr_result")
})
tr2 <- hr_trace()
go <- function(prompt, label) {
  hr_call(cut_off, prompt, model = "reasoner", trace = tr2, label = label, effort = pol2)
}
go("Write a long draft.", "draft")$finish_reason
go("Review the draft.", "review")$text
hr_effort_event(tr2, "disagreement", note = "the two reviewers differ")
go("Write the final text.", "final")$text
go("Polish the wording.", "polish")$text
hr_effort_log(tr2)
```

The draft was cut off at its cap, the `"truncated"` trigger, so the review
went out at xhigh. During the review, the code reported a disagreement, so the
final stage went out raised too. That was the second and last raise, so
`polish` went back to its base of medium. Both raises resolved: each raised
stage fired none of the triggers that raised it. A third trigger would have
raised nothing.

`hr_effort_event()` returns `TRUE` when it recorded the event, invisibly, so
the call in the chunk above printed nothing. It records nothing, and returns
`FALSE`, on a trace no escalation policy has sent a request on, so a run
without a policy records nothing new:

```{r}
print(hr_effort_event(hr_trace(), "disagreement"))
```

A reply to `hr_call(schema = )` that is not JSON is a trigger only when your
code reports it. This policy narrows `on` to `"parse_failure"`, so no other
trigger raises a stage:

```{r}
pol3 <- hr_effort_escalate(base = "low", to = "high", on = "parse_failure")
extractor <- hr_mock_client(function(messages, params) {
  if (identical(params$effort, "low")) "Revenue was 45.2." else '{"revenue": 45.2}'
})
revenue_schema <- list(type = "object",
                       properties = list(revenue = list(type = "number")),
                       required = list("revenue"))
tr3 <- hr_trace()
ask <- function(label) {
  hr_call(extractor, "Give the revenue as JSON.", model = "reasoner", trace = tr3,
          label = label, effort = pol3, schema = revenue_schema, schema_name = "revenue")
}
first <- ask("extract")
first$text
if (!jsonlite::validate(first$text)) {
  print(hr_effort_event(tr3, "parse_failure", label = "extract"))
}
ask("extract_again")$text
hr_effort_log(tr3)[, c("after", "stage", "to", "resolved")]
```

The first reply came back as prose, `jsonlite::validate()` found it was not
JSON, and the code reported `"parse_failure"`, which printed `TRUE`. The next stage went out at high and returned
JSON, so the raise resolved.

### What escalation does not do

- It does not send a stage again. The stage that fired a trigger keeps its
  replies; the raise applies to the stage after it. To retry a request at a
  higher effort, call again with that effort yourself.
- It does not change the effort part way through a stage.
- It does not raise more often than `max_escalations` allows, and a run's
  state lives on its trace, so two runs on two traces raise separately.
- It has not been shown to keep accuracy. Measure that on your own task,
  as the next section does.

## Does more effort pay? `hr_effort_check()` {#check}

A policy that starts low pays off if it answers as well as a fixed effort and
costs less. `hr_effort_check()` tests the first part with the non-inferiority
test of `hr_report()` and reports the cost of each arm, with the raised
requests counted. It reads a benchmark you build with `hr_benchmark()`;
`vignette("evaluate")` covers benchmarks, references and the test.

The benchmark below has three arms of one two-stage task: a fixed `"low"`, a
fixed `"high"` and the escalation policy. Each arm reads its effort from its
`params`, which is one way to hold a run's effort in one place. In the
stand-in, five of the hundred items are hard: at low effort the first stage
finds nothing and the answer is wrong. Reasoning costs 100 tokens a request at
low and 1,500 at high:

```{r}
ref <- hr_reference(sprintf("q%03d", 1:100), labels = rep("yes", 100),
                    cluster = sprintf("c%02d", rep(1:50, each = 2)), split = "test")
task <- function(item, ctx) {
  e <- ctx$params$effort
  hr_call(ctx$client, paste("find", item), model = "reasoner", trace = ctx$trace,
          label = "task.find", effort = e)
  hr_call(ctx$client, paste("answer", item), model = "reasoner", trace = ctx$trace,
          label = "task.answer", effort = e)$text
}
esc <- hr_effort_escalate(replies = c(not_in_document = "NOT FOUND"))
arms <- list(hr_arm("low", task, params = list(effort = "low")),
             hr_arm("high", task, params = list(effort = "high")),
             hr_arm("escalate", task, params = list(effort = esc)))

reasoning_at <- c(low = 100L, high = 1500L)
provider <- hr_backend_client(function(messages, params) {
  q <- messages[[1]]$content
  hard <- grepl("q00[1-5]", q) && identical(params$effort, "low")
  text <- if (!hard) "yes" else if (startsWith(q, "find")) "NOT FOUND" else "no"
  r <- reasoning_at[[params$effort]]
  structure(list(ok = TRUE, text = text,
                 usage = list(input = 50L, output = r + 2L, reasoning = r,
                              provenance = "reported")),
            class = "gr_result")
})
bench <- hr_benchmark(arms, ref, runs = 5, client = provider,
                      governor = hr_governor(max_calls = 4000, max_cost_usd = 50))
chk <- hr_effort_check(bench, "escalate", margin = 0.10, B = 500)
chk
```

The first block tests the policy against each fixed effort: every other arm,
since `comparators` was left out. `margin` is the largest loss of accuracy you
accept, here 10 points, and the policy is non-inferior to an arm when the lower
bound of the difference stays above minus the margin. The bounds come from
`B` bootstrap resamples drawn with `seed` (1 by default), and Holm's procedure
adjusts the tests for there being more than one comparison. "best fixed
comparator" names the most accurate of the fixed arms, the one the policy most
needs to match. The cost table gives, per arm, the accuracy, the mean cost
per run (`usd`), the requests per run (`calls`), the raises per run
(`escalations`), the requests sent raised per run (`escalated_calls`) and the
share of raises that resolved. Its last three columns say where `usd`'s prices
came from: `priced` is `TRUE` when every run's models have a price, `as_of` is
the oldest month among those prices, and `certain` is `TRUE` when every
model's registry entry is a fact rather than a guess from a pattern.

Here the policy answered every item, as `"high"` did, at about a tenth of
its cost: only the hard items' answer stage went out raised. Against `"low"`
it is "not shown" for the other part of the test. By default (`cost_test =
TRUE`) a verdict also needs the policy to cost less than the arm it replaces,
with the upper bound of the cost difference below zero, and it costs more
than a fixed `"low"`:

```{r}
chk$contrasts[, c("reference", "estimate", "lower", "accuracy_holds",
                  "cost_diff", "cost_holds", "verdict")]
```

With `cost_test = FALSE`, the verdict rests on accuracy alone. Here it is run
against `"high"` alone, through `comparators`:

```{r}
chk_acc <- hr_effort_check(bench, "escalate", comparators = "high", margin = 0.10,
                           cost_test = FALSE, B = 500)
chk_acc$contrasts[, c("reference", "estimate", "lower", "accuracy_holds", "verdict")]
```

With one comparison, Holm's procedure has nothing to adjust, and the verdict
follows the accuracy test.

The header says "post hoc": the margin was chosen after the benchmark was
scored, so the result is evidence for running a registered comparison, not a
verdict. Register the contrasts and margin with `hr_register_contrasts()`
before the benchmark runs and pass them as `registration`, as
`vignette("evaluate")` shows; the check then tests those contrasts at their
registered margins. Either way the benchmark's rows must be on the test or
final split.

`hr_effort_check()` plans nothing: the arms, the items and the runs are yours.
The stand-in makes the policy look good by design, so run the check on your
own task before you change a default.

## Choosing the settings

Two settings belong to effort: the option `reasoning_floor`, and
`effort_mode`, a setting of a document read. Each walkthrough says what the
setting controls, the signs that point to changing it, where its default came
from and how to test a change.

### The output cap floor: `reasoning_floor` {#set-reasoning-floor}

**What it controls.** The smallest output cap an HTTP request to a reasoning
model is sent with, 2,048 tokens by default. A call that asks for a smaller
cap is sent with the floor instead, held to the model's output limit and to
the room the context window leaves after the prompt. A cap at or above the
floor is sent as it is, and `0` turns the raise off. It trades a short
request's spend for room to reason: without it, a call that asks for 100
tokens can spend all 100 reasoning and return nothing.

**Signs it needs changing.** Short structured requests to a reasoning model
that come back cut off, with `finish_reason` `"length"`, `tokens_reasoning`
near the cap and no text, point to a higher floor. Requests that use far less
than the floor at the effort you send, on a model that bills by tokens used,
need no change, since unused cap costs nothing; a lower floor matters only
when the spending limits refuse requests checked at the raised cap.

**Where the default came from.** The constant the code had before the option
existed, from the observation that a reasoning model can spend a few hundred
to a couple of thousand tokens before it replies. It was not measured, and
`gr_settings_table("options")` lists it as untested.

**How to test it.** A value other than the default joins the response cache
key, so replies cached at one floor are not reused at another:

```{r}
hr_call(cached, "What was revenue?", model = "reasoner", effort = "low")$cached
prev <- hr_options(reasoning_floor = 4096)
hr_call(cached, "What was revenue?", model = "reasoner", effort = "low")$cached
hr_options(prev)
```

The same request was answered from the cache at the default floor and missed
at 4,096. The floor joins the key for every model, not only the reasoning
ones, because the key records the option and not what it did to a request.

Then run your short requests at each floor you consider with a real client,
and compare `finish_reason`, `tokens_reasoning` and the trace's
`params_sent$max_output`:

```{r eval = FALSE}
hr_options(reasoning_floor = 4096)
tr <- hr_trace()
res <- hr_call(hr_client(), "Score this passage from 0 to 10.", model = "gpt-5.6-luna",
               max_output = 50, effort = "medium", trace = tr, label = "score")
c(res$finish_reason, res$usage$reasoning)
tr$steps[[1]]$params_sent$max_output
```

### Effort that rises when needed: `effort_mode` {#set-effort-mode}

**What it controls.** `effort_mode` is a setting of `gr_read_spec()`. With
`effort_mode = "escalate"`, a read starts every stage at its `effort` (`"low"`
when `effort` is unset). It sends the next stage
at `"high"` when one of these went wrong in the stage before:

- a cut;
- a reply stopped at its output cap;
- a reply that is not the JSON asked for;
- `NOT_IN_DOCUMENT` from every request of the stage;
- a quotation `iterative` could not verify;
- `ensemble` members that disagree.

Effort changes only at a stage boundary, at most once a read, and the stage
after a raised one goes back to the base effort. The setting trades the cost of
reasoning at a high effort on every request against the cost of a wrong answer
where low effort was not enough. A raise costs nothing but the raised stage's
reasoning.

**Signs it needs changing.** Look for a fixed `"high"` effort whose bill is
mostly reasoning on requests that a low effort answers as well, or for answers
at a fixed `"low"` that come back cut off, unparsed or not found. The trace
records each raise as an `"effort.escalate"` step. `hr_effort_log()` shows
which trigger fired and whether the raised stage fired it again.

**Where the default came from.** `"static"` sends the effort `effort` names, as
harnessr did before the setting existed; the settings table marks it
`untested`. No one has compared escalation with a fixed effort here, and
`hr_effort_check()` makes that comparison.

**How to test it.** `qa` below holds one question about the example report.
`refine` reads the report with a stand-in reasoning model that, at low effort,
finds nothing in the first chunk, where `refine` drafts its answer:

```{r}
qa <- gr_qa_reference(questions = c(revenue = "What was revenue in 2024?"),
                      documents = gr_example(), answers = list("45.2 million"),
                      split = "dev")
hr_register_model("priced-reasoner", context_window = 128000, max_output = 8192,
                  input_usd = 1, output_usd = 4, reasoning = TRUE)
thinks <- hr_mock_client(function(messages, params) {
  if (identical(params$effort, "low") &&
      startsWith(messages[[2]]$content, "<excerpts>")) {
    return("NOT_IN_DOCUMENT")
  }
  "Revenue was 45.2 million dollars."
})
efforts <- hr_sweep(function(effort) {
  gr_arm("thorough", list(method = "sentence", max_tokens = 150, overlap_tokens = 0,
                          model = "priced-reasoner", reader = "refine",
                          effort = if (effort != "escalate") effort,
                          effort_mode = if (effort == "escalate") "escalate" else "static"))
}, list(effort = c("low", "high", "escalate")))
eb <- hr_benchmark(efforts, qa, runs = 5, client = thinks, split = "dev",
                   scorer = gr_scorer_answer(),
                   governor = hr_governor(max_calls = 200, max_cost_usd = 1))
sent <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(nrow(eb)), function(i) {
  d <- as.data.frame(attr(eb, "traces")[[eb$ledger_id[i]]])
  d <- d[!is.na(d$effort), ]
  data.frame(arm = eb$arm[i], stage = d$stage, effort = d$effort)
}))
table(sent$arm, paste(sent$stage, sent$effort))
hr_effort_log(attr(eb, "traces")[[eb$ledger_id[eb$arm == "thorough:effort=escalate"][1]]])
```

At `"low"` every request went out low, and at `"high"` every one went out high.
Under `"escalate"` the draft went out low and found nothing. That raised the
four revisions after it to high, and the log shows that the raise resolved the
trigger: the revisions found the figure.

Four of the five requests of each run went out raised here, because the draft
is one request. On a reader whose first stage is many requests (`map_reduce`'s
chunks), the raised stage is the smaller share.

`hr_effort_check()` reads a benchmark of such arms with the non-inferiority test
of `hr_report()`, as [Does more effort pay?](#check) shows. That test needs a
reference with a test split and enough items and runs for intervals, which `qa`
lacks, so run the check on a benchmark of your own:

```{r eval = FALSE}
chk <- hr_effort_check(your_bench, candidate = "thorough:effort=escalate", margin = 0.05)
chk$contrasts[, c("reference", "estimate", "lower", "verdict")]
chk$cost
```

Register the margin with `hr_register_contrasts()` before the benchmark runs
and pass it as `registration`; without one, the result is marked post hoc.

## Where the document layer builds on this {#document-layer}

A read takes an effort map as the `effort` setting of `gr_read_spec()`, and
its `effort_mode = "escalate"` builds an `hr_effort_escalate()` policy from it,
as the [`effort_mode` walkthrough](#set-effort-mode) above shows. "Reasoning
effort, stage by stage" in `vignette("readers")` lists each reader's labels.

In a review, the same vector goes to each stage. `gr_screen()` and
`gr_extract()` take it as a recipe override; `gr_claims()`, `gr_outline()` and
`gr_synthesise()` take it as an argument. With
`effort = c(extract = "low", synthesise = "high")`, the per-chunk extraction
stays cheap and the spending goes to the writing.

The document layer checks the names of a map against the labels its readers
declare. A name that matches no declared call stops with an error of class
`hr_unknown_effort_key` that lists the stems. A misspelt `c(extrac = "low")`
therefore cannot send every extraction at the provider's default unnoticed, as
it can through `hr_call()` (see
[One effort for every call, or one per stage](#one-effort-for-every-call-or-one-per-stage)).
`?gr_read_spec` lists every label and suggests a profile: low for the many
per-chunk calls, high for the few that judge.

```{r include = FALSE}
hr_cache_clear(cache)
hr_options(old)
```
